what_its_for: Trastuzumab-qyyp is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of breast cancer and stomach cancer that have too much of a protein called HER2. It works by attaching to HER2 proteins on cancer cells and helping your immune system attack and slow the growth of those cancer cells.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you through an IV (intravenous) infusion directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion session usually takes about 30 to 90 minutes. Your healthcare team will watch you closely during and after each infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body weight in kilograms. The usual starting dose is 8 mg per kg of body weight given over 90 minutes as your first infusion. After that, you will receive a maintenance dose of 6 mg per kg every 3 weeks, or 2 mg per kg every week, depending on your treatment plan. Your doctor will decide the exact schedule that is right for you and your type of cancer.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given to you in a clinic, your healthcare team will help schedule all of your appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Do not wait until your next scheduled visit. It is very important to stay on your treatment schedule for the medicine to work properly.
storage: You will not store this medicine at home. The clinic or pharmacy prepares and stores it for you. If you are given any information about take-home supplies or other related medicines, store those exactly as your healthcare team instructs you.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant before starting treatment. This medicine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby, so use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. Avoid getting live vaccines while on this treatment without talking to your doctor first. Let all of your healthcare providers know you are taking this medicine before any new treatments, surgeries, or procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, or wheezing; chest pain or tightness; irregular or fast heartbeat; swelling of your ankles, feet, or legs; sudden weight gain of more than 5 pounds in a day or two; severe dizziness or fainting; fever, chills, or shaking during or after your infusion; nausea, vomiting, or flushing that feels severe; any signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, rash, itching, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat. Also tell your doctor if you feel unusually tired, notice a cough that is new or getting worse, or feel your heart is racing or pounding.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away after your first infusion, but you may not feel or see changes immediately. Cancer treatment takes time. Your doctor will check how well the medicine is working through regular tests, scans, and check-ups. Some patients begin to see results within a few weeks to months. It is important to keep all of your appointments even if you feel well, because the medicine needs to be given on a regular schedule to be most effective.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. It can cause harm or death to an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 7 months after stopping. If you become pregnant during treatment, tell your doctor immediately. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. Heart problems: Tell your doctor if you have ever had heart disease, heart failure, or if you have received certain other cancer medicines that affect the heart. Your doctor will monitor your heart function regularly during treatment. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more likely to experience certain side effects, especially heart-related ones, and will be monitored closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions you have, as your dose or monitoring may need to be adjusted.
